sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
Shortly before six on a winter morning, by Indian Standard Time, the sun clears the ridges above **Dong**, a village of a few dozen people at the point where India, China and Myanmar meet. It is the first sunlight to touch India. For the new year of 2026 the state held its first Sunrise Festival there.

The same ridges are drawn twice on the world's maps. India's map shows them as Arunachal Pradesh, a state since 1987. China's map shows them as **Zangnan**, 'south Tibet', and since 2017 Beijing has issued Chinese names for dozens of its villages, rivers and peaks.

In between these two facts lives a place most Indians never visit. It is as big as Austria and holds fewer people than Lucknow. Its people speak more than thirty languages and talk to each other in Hindi. It has a Buddhist monastery that once sheltered the Dalai Lama, a valley where rice and fish grow in the same water, and a forest with four kinds of big cat. Today you meet it through what you can see.

sections.title: Where you are
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal Pradesh is the north-eastern corner of India: a wedge of the eastern Himalaya between Bhutan in the west, Tibet in the north and Myanmar in the east, with Assam and Nagaland along its southern foothills. It runs from about 100 metres above sea level on the Assam plain to more than 7,000 metres on the Tibetan border.

Its name was coined in 1972, when the North-East Frontier Agency became a Union Territory. It means, roughly, **land of the dawn-lit mountains**. Full statehood came on **20 February 1987**, and the 40th Statehood Day was celebrated in Itanagar in February 2026.

Six numbers carry the place. 83,743 square kilometres. 1.38 million people in 2011. 17 people per square kilometre, the emptiest state in India. Two in three people belong to a Scheduled Tribe. About 77 per cent of the land is under trees. And a 1,129-kilometre border with China that has never been agreed.

sections.title: The land
sections.intro_md:
Five big rivers cut Arunachal into long north-south valleys: from west to east the **Kameng**, the **Subansiri**, the **Siang**, the **Dibang** and the **Lohit**. They all end in the Brahmaputra on the Assam plain. Between them the ridges climb fast, so a day's drive can take you from tropical forest with wild elephants to alpine lakes that freeze in winter.

Rain is the second fact of the land: 2,000 to 5,000 millimetres a year, most of it between May and October. Roads wash out every monsoon. The great earthquake of 15 August 1950, centred just over the border in Tibet, threw down whole hillsides and reshaped rivers.

The highest point is **Kangto**, about 7,060 metres, on the disputed line north of East Kameng. The lowest forests, around Namdapha and Pakke, are among the richest in Asia.

spotlights.name: Dong, the first sunrise
spotlights.spot_it: A cluster of huts on a ridge above the Lohit river, where photographers wait in the dark on 31 December.
spotlights.story_md: Dong sits at about 1,240 metres in Anjaw district, near the tri-junction of India, China and Myanmar. Because it is the easternmost inhabited corner of the country, the sun reaches it before anywhere else in India, around an hour earlier than in Gujarat. India runs on one time zone, so by Indian Standard Time the sun rises at about 6 in midwinter and around 4 in June, and people in the east have long asked for their own time. From 29 December 2025 to 2 January 2026 the state held its first Sunrise Festival at Dong, opened by Chief Minister Pema Khandu with Meyor rituals of the local community. The road there passes Walong, where Indian troops fought in 1962.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The one place where India's single time zone visibly does not fit.
spotlights.memory_hook: India wakes up in Dong while Delhi is still dark.

spotlights.name: Sela Pass and Sela Lake
spotlights.spot_it: A prayer-flag gate at about 4,170 metres, with a dark lake beside the road that freezes white in winter.
spotlights.story_md: Every vehicle bound for Tawang used to cross Sela Pass, about 4,170 metres up, often in snow. The lake beside it is sacred to Buddhists, and about a hundred smaller lakes dot the plateau around it. The pass carries a story from 1962: it is said to be named after **Sela**, a Monpa girl who brought food and water to the rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat during his last stand nearby, and who died in the fighting. Since March 2024 a tunnel under the pass keeps the road open in winter, but tourists still drive up to the lake.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The gateway to Tawang, and a war story told through a place name.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lake, a pass and a tunnel, all named for one girl.

spotlights.name: The Siang: the Brahmaputra coming home
spotlights.spot_it: A wide grey-green river spilling out of the hills at Pasighat onto sandbars and the Assam plain.
spotlights.story_md: The Siang begins as the **Yarlung Tsangpo** in Tibet, flows east for over a thousand kilometres, then turns south around the 7,782-metre peak Namcha Barwa through the deepest canyon on land, up to about 6,000 metres deep. It enters India in Upper Siang, drops through Adi country, and at Pasighat meets the plain. There it joins the Dibang and Lohit and becomes the Brahmaputra. For decades nobody in Europe could prove the Tsangpo and the Brahmaputra were one river. The Adi call it Siang; Assam calls it Dihang.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One river ties Tibet, Arunachal and Assam, which is why dams on it are a diplomatic issue.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tsangpo in Tibet, Siang in Arunachal, Brahmaputra in Assam: one river, three names.

spotlights.name: Namdapha
spotlights.spot_it: Dense lowland rainforest climbing to snow peaks, crossed by the Noa-Dihing river.
spotlights.story_md: Namdapha National Park in Changlang district covers about 1,985 square kilometres and rises from about 200 metres to 4,571 metres. That climb packs tropical forest, temperate forest and alpine meadow into one park, and it is the reason Namdapha holds four big cats: the tiger, the leopard, the clouded leopard and the snow leopard. It also has the hoolock gibbon and about 425 bird species. One resident is a mystery: the Namdapha flying squirrel, known from a single specimen collected in 1981 and not confirmed since. A gliding lizard, Draco, sails between its trees.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of very few places on Earth where four big cats share a single park.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tiger at the bottom, snow leopard at the top, same park.

spotlights.name: Mechuka
spotlights.spot_it: A wide, flat valley with a meandering river and a wooden monastery on the slope above.
spotlights.story_md: Mechuka lies about 1,900 metres up in Shi Yomi district, 29 kilometres from the line with China. The name is often explained as 'medicinal water' in the local Memba language. The valley is home to Memba Buddhists and to Ramo and Bokar people of the Adi group, and the Samten Yongcha monastery on the hill is said to be around 400 years old. For decades the main link to the outside world was an Advanced Landing Ground, revived by the Indian Air Force in 2016. It has become one of Arunachal's newest tourist valleys, with snow in winter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how the border valleys are being pulled into India's road and air network.
spotlights.memory_hook: A meadow at the end of the road, 29 km from China.

sections.title: Wild things
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal sits where three great regions of life overlap: the Himalaya, the forests of Southeast Asia and the plains of India. That is why a state with fewer people than many Indian cities keeps finding animals that science had never described. A new macaque was announced in 2004, a new bird in 2006, a new gibbon subspecies in 2013.

Most of the forest is not in national parks. It belongs to villages and clans, and hunting is part of culture. So conservation here works best when it pays people and respects them, as the hornbill programme around Pakke shows.

The state animal is the **mithun**, a domestic animal that lives half wild. The state bird is the great hornbill, and the state tree is the hollong, a tall rainforest giant.

spotlights.name: Great hornbill
spotlights.spot_it: A huge black-and-white bird with a yellow casque on its bill, whose wingbeats sound like a steam engine.
spotlights.story_md: Great hornbills nest in holes in tall trees. The female seals herself inside with mud and droppings, leaving a slit, and the male feeds her and the chicks through it for months. Around **Pakke Tiger Reserve** the Nyishi traditionally hunted hornbills for their beaks and meat. Since 2011 the Nature Conservation Foundation, the Ghora-Aabhe society of village heads and the forest department have run a **Hornbill Nest Adoption Programme**: people in cities pay to 'adopt' a nest, and the money pays local Nyishi men to guard it. In 2016 the reserve won the India Biodiversity Award for it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that a hunting culture can become a guarding culture when it is paid and respected.
spotlights.memory_hook: The father feeds his family through a slit in a mud wall.

spotlights.name: Mithun
spotlights.spot_it: A big black bovine with white stockings and flat, thick horns, grazing loose in the forest.
spotlights.story_md: The mithun, or gayal, is the state animal of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland. It was domesticated from the wild gaur, probably more than 8,000 years ago, but it still lives half wild: herds roam the forest on their own and come back to the village when called, often for a lick of salt. A mithun is wealth. It is paid as a fine, sacrificed at feasts and given in marriage; among the Adi, a marriage is not settled until the groom's family gives the bride's household at least one. India has a National Research Centre on Mithun, in Nagaland.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A walking bank account that explains much about village economics.
spotlights.memory_hook: No mithun, no wedding.

spotlights.name: Mishmi takin
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy, golden-brown goat-antelope with a thick nose and swept-back horns, like a moose crossed with a goat.
spotlights.story_md: The takin lives in the high forests of the Mishmi Hills and the Dibang valley, and the Mishmi takin is a subspecies found in this corner of the Himalaya. It looks clumsy but climbs steep bamboo slopes with ease and moves to salt licks in summer. The Mishmi Hills around it have about 6,000 plant species and roughly 680 bird species, and a new subspecies of hoolock gibbon was described from them in 2013. Takins are hunted for meat, and dams planned in the Dibang valley would flood parts of their range.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Flags the Mishmi Hills as one of the least explored biodiversity hotspots in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half moose, half goat, all Mishmi.

spotlights.name: Hoolock gibbon
spotlights.spot_it: A long-armed tailless ape swinging through the canopy, its whooping song carrying across the valley at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: Gibbons are apes, not monkeys: no tail, long arms, and a habit of swinging hand over hand through the trees. The hoolock gibbons of the Northeast are the **only apes in India**. Males are black with white eyebrows; adult females are a pale buff. Pairs sing loud duets at dawn to mark their patch of forest. In Arunachal they live in Namdapha, the Mishmi Hills and the Lohit forests. They need unbroken canopy, so roads and jhum clearings that cut the forest trap them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's only ape lives in these forests.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's only ape sings duets at dawn.

spotlights.name: Red panda
spotlights.spot_it: A rust-red, cat-sized animal with a ringed tail, asleep on a high branch of a fir or rhododendron.
spotlights.story_md: The red panda lives in temperate forests between about 2,200 and 4,800 metres, with thick bamboo underneath. It eats mostly bamboo leaves and spends much of the day asleep in trees. Western Arunachal, around Tawang and West Kameng, holds part of India's population, alongside Sikkim and Darjeeling. It is endangered across its range because its forests are cut and broken up, and because it is caught for the pet trade in neighbouring countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A flagship for the high forests that also feed the state's rivers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bamboo-eater, branch-sleeper, not a bear.

spotlights.name: Bugun liocichla
spotlights.spot_it: A small olive bird with a black cap, yellow-orange eyebrow and red patches on the wing, in roadside scrub.
spotlights.story_md: The Bugun liocichla was first glimpsed in 1995 in Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, then lost for ten years. In January 2005 **Ramana Athreya**, an astrophysicist and birdwatcher, found it again, and in 2006 described it as a new species without killing a single bird: feathers, photos and sound recordings served as the type. He named it after the Bugun people, on whose community forest it lives. One survey counted just 14 birds, and only a few breeding pairs are known. It is critically endangered.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A bird new to science in 2006, named after the people who protect its forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: An astronomer found a new bird and named it for a tribe.

spotlights.name: Arunachal macaque
spotlights.spot_it: A stocky brown monkey with a short tail and a dark face, in the high forests around Tawang.
spotlights.story_md: In 2003 and 2004, a team from the National Institute of Advanced Studies, the Nature Conservation Foundation and the Wildlife Conservation Society photographed a stocky, dark-faced macaque in Tawang and West Kameng that did not match any known species. In 2005 they described it as **Macaca munzala**, the Arunachal macaque, using the Dirang Monpa name munzala, 'deep-forest monkey'. Surveys in 2004 and 2005 found at least 569 animals in 35 troops, living between about 2,000 and 3,500 metres, often raiding crops.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first new macaque species described in a century, named with a local word.
spotlights.memory_hook: A new monkey, named in Monpa.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
With 1.38 million people in 2011, Arunachal had roughly the population of a mid-sized Indian city spread over an area larger than Punjab. Only 22.9 per cent lived in towns. Itanagar, the capital, is the largest urban area.

The state is officially counted as **26 major tribes and more than 100 sub-tribes**, though the lists are argued over. Scheduled Tribes made up 68.8 per cent of the population in 2011, eight times the national share. The rest include people from Assam, Bihar, Nepal and elsewhere who came as traders, soldiers, labourers and teachers, and the Chakma and Hajong refugees settled here in the 1960s, whose citizenship is still a live political issue.

Sex ratio was 938 women per 1,000 men in 2011, close to India's 943. Literacy was about 65 per cent, below India's 74, though it has been rising fast.

sections.title: Deep history
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal has no single old kingdom of its own. For most of history the hill peoples governed themselves by village and clan, and wrote nothing down. What we know comes from oral history, from Tibetan, Ahom and British records, and from ruins in the foothills.

In the west, Monyul, the land of the Monpa, came under Tibetan influence from about the 7th century, and Tibetan Buddhism took root. In the foothills of the east, the **Chutia kings** of upper Assam built brick forts and stone temples in the 13th to 15th centuries. The Ahom kingdom later dealt with the hill peoples by paying them a share of plains produce, called posa, in return for peace. The British inherited that arrangement after the First Anglo-Burmese War of 1824 to 1826, and then, from 1873, drew an Inner Line that kept plains people out.

spotlights.name: Bhismaknagar
spotlights.spot_it: Long walls of fired brick in the jungle near Roing, with the outline of a palace platform.
spotlights.story_md: Bhismaknagar, in Lower Dibang Valley near Roing, is the largest archaeological site in Arunachal. Its walls of fired brick, up to about 4.5 metres high in places, enclose a fort and palace complex built by the Chutia kings, who ruled upper Assam until the 16th century. Local legend connects it to King Bhishmaka, father of Rukmini in the Mahabharata. Among the finds is a terracotta tile showing a man with what looks like a **hand-cannon**, a hint that gunpowder weapons reached this corner of Asia early. Ita Fort in the capital belongs to the same brick-building world; 'ita' means brick, and Itanagar is named after it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows that the eastern foothills were part of a brick-building, plains-linked state long before the British.
spotlights.memory_hook: A brick palace in the jungle, and a terracotta man with a gun.

spotlights.name: Malinithan
spotlights.spot_it: Granite sculptures of gods on animals laid out on a low hill above the Brahmaputra plain.
spotlights.story_md: Malinithan, at Likabali in Lower Siang district, is a ruined stone temple on a hill about 21 metres high, dated by archaeologists to around the 13th century. Excavations uncovered a carved plinth and granite sculptures: Indra on his elephant Airavata, Kartikeya on a peacock, Surya on a chariot, Ganesha on a mouse and a big Nandi bull. The legend says Krishna and Rukmini rested here while eloping, and Shiva and Durga, who were living on the hill, welcomed them; Parvati gave Krishna a garland of flowers, hence 'Malini'. The Assamese saint Sankardev spread the story in the 16th century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hindu stone art at the very edge of the Himalaya, made for a plains kingdom.
spotlights.memory_hook: Krishna eloped, the goddess gave him a garland: Malinithan.

spotlights.name: Tsangyang Gyatso, the 6th Dalai Lama
spotlights.spot_it: A small monastery among oak trees at Urgelling, 5 km from Tawang, with a stone footprint said to be his.
spotlights.story_md: Tsangyang Gyatso was born on 1 March 1683 at Urgelling, near Tawang, to a Monpa mother. The 5th Dalai Lama had died in 1682, and his regent kept the death secret for years. When the search for the next incarnation came, monks looked for a valley whose name ended in 'ling'. The boy was taken to Lhasa in 1697. He turned out to prefer archery, wine and women to monastic life, and he wrote **love songs** that are still sung across the Tibetan world. Deposed in 1706, he disappeared that November, probably dying on the way to China.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tawang's tie to Tibet runs through a poet who refused to be a monk.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Dalai Lama who wrote love songs was born near Tawang.

spotlights.name: Kinthup and the 500 logs
spotlights.spot_it: Imagine a man on a Tibetan riverbank throwing marked logs into the water, with no one waiting downstream.
spotlights.story_md: In 1880 the Survey of India sent **Kinthup**, a Lepcha tailor from Sikkim, into Tibet with a Chinese lama to settle a question: did the Tsangpo become the Brahmaputra? The lama sold him as a slave in 1881. He escaped, was caught and sold again to a monastery, and finally bought his freedom. Still on mission, he cut 500 logs, marked them, and threw them into the Tsangpo in batches, after sending a letter asking for watchers on the Brahmaputra. His officer, Captain Harman, had died; nobody read the letter or watched the river. Kinthup returned in 1884 and was not believed. In 1913 Bailey and Morshead proved him right.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The proof that the Siang is the Brahmaputra cost one man four years of his life.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five hundred logs floated past, and nobody was watching.

sections.title: The border and the war
sections.intro_md:
In 1913 and 1914, British, Tibetan and Chinese delegates met at Simla. The British negotiator, Henry McMahon, and the Tibetan representative agreed a line along the crest of the Himalaya, drawn in red on a map. China's delegate initialled the draft and was then disowned by his government. That **McMahon Line**, about 890 kilometres long, put Tawang inside British India. Britain did little with it for decades.

After independence, India pushed administration up to the line and set up the **North-East Frontier Agency** (NEFA) in 1954. China never accepted the line. On 20 October 1962 Chinese forces attacked. In a month they took Tawang, came over Sela and down to Bomdila, and reached the foothills of Assam. Then, on 21 November, China declared a ceasefire and withdrew to roughly the McMahon Line. The border today is the Line of Actual Control, and China still claims about 90,000 square kilometres, nearly the whole state.

spotlights.name: The McMahon Line
spotlights.spot_it: A thick red line on a 1914 map along the Himalayan crest, signed by a Briton and a Tibetan.
spotlights.story_md: The line Henry McMahon drew in 1914 followed the highest ridges and watersheds from Bhutan to Burma. Tibet accepted it in a separate exchange of notes; China did not sign the convention. For India it is the international border, inherited from Britain. For China it is an illegal colonial line, and the land south of it is 'south Tibet'. The map was drawn at a scale where the thickness of the pen covered kilometres on the ground, so even the two sides' versions of the line differ in places such as Thag La. That vagueness fed the war of 1962 and still causes clashes, such as at Yangtse near Tawang in December 2022.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Almost every argument about Arunachal goes back to this line.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pen line that is kilometres wide on the ground.

spotlights.name: Jaswant Singh Rawat and Jaswantgarh
spotlights.spot_it: A memorial at Nuranang, on the Tawang road below Sela, where soldiers still keep a room for a dead rifleman.
spotlights.story_md: On 17 November 1962, at Nuranang, Rifleman **Jaswant Singh Rawat** of 4 Garhwal Rifles and two comrades crawled up to a Chinese machine gun that was cutting down his company and captured it; the other two were killed. When his company withdrew, the story goes, he stayed and fought for about 72 hours, helped by two Monpa girls, **Sela** and **Nura**. Sela was killed and Nura captured. How Jaswant died is unclear. He received the Maha Vir Chakra after death, and the army treats him as if he were still serving: at the Jaswantgarh memorial his bed is made and his boots polished.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most loved soldier legend of the 1962 war, told along the Tawang road.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sela Pass and Nuranang Falls are named after the two girls who helped him.

spotlights.name: The Stilwell Road
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow road climbing from Assam through Jairampur to Pangsau Pass and the Burmese border.
spotlights.story_md: In December 1942 American army engineers began a road from Ledo in Assam over the Patkai hills into Burma, to supply China after Japan cut the old Burma Road. About 15,000 American soldiers, roughly 60 per cent of them African-American, and about 35,000 local workers built it through jungle, monsoon mud and malaria. The first convoy left Ledo on 12 January 1945 and reached Kunming on 4 February. More than 1,100 Americans died, giving the phrase 'a man a mile'. About 61 km of the road lie in India, through Changlang district, past a war cemetery near Jairampur, to the Pangsau Pass and the Lake of No Return.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Arunachal's corner was a front line of the Second World War.
spotlights.memory_hook: A man a mile, from Ledo to Kunming.

spotlights.name: Verrier Elwin and the philosophy for NEFA
spotlights.spot_it: His 1959 map of NEFA, and his own 1950s photographs of hill people, now in the RIWATCH museum.
spotlights.story_md: Verrier Elwin came to India in 1927 as a missionary, left the church, lived for two decades among the Gonds and Baigas of central India, and became an Indian citizen. In 1954 Nehru made him adviser on tribal affairs for NEFA. In his book *A Philosophy for NEFA* (1959) Elwin argued for development at the people's own pace: protect land and forests, work through village councils, keep outsiders and missionaries out, and do not force a plains way of life on the hills. Nehru set out five principles in the same spirit. Critics called it a museum policy; defenders say it is why land in Arunachal is still mostly owned by its people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Explains the Inner Line Permit, tribal land laws and the slow, protected opening of the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nehru's Englishman who said: let the hills set their own pace.

sections.title: The peoples
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal's peoples belong to several large families, and the differences between them are as big as those between European nations. The **Tani** peoples of the centre (Nyishi, Adi, Galo, Apatani, Tagin) trace descent from a common ancestor, Abo Tani, and pray to the sun and moon. The **Monpa** and **Sherdukpen** of the west are Buddhists of the Tibetan tradition. The **Mishmi** live in the Dibang and Lohit valleys. In the south-east, the **Tangsa, Nocte and Wancho** are related to the Naga peoples. The **Tai Khamti** and **Singpho** of the eastern plains are Theravada Buddhists linked to Myanmar.

Many groups once lived by jhum, shifting cultivation, and organised life through village councils, men's dormitories and clan law. Nearly all of that survives in some form, reshaped by schools, roads, churches, revival movements and phones.

spotlights.name: Apatani of Ziro
spotlights.spot_it: Older women with blue facial tattoos and round black plugs in the sides of the nose.
spotlights.story_md: About 44,000 Apatani live in the Ziro valley, Lower Subansiri. Their older women are the most photographed people in the state, for facial tattoos (a line from forehead to nose tip and stripes on the chin) and cane **nose plugs**, called yaping hurlo. Local stories say the marks were meant to make women less attractive to raiders from neighbouring tribes; other accounts call them simply marks of beauty and identity. In 1974 the Apatani Youth Association called for the practices to end, and girls born after the early 1970s were not marked. Within a generation the last tattooed grandmothers will be gone.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living custom you can still see, and a deliberate decision by a community to end it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nose plugs stopped in the 1970s: the last generation is now in its sixties and older.

spotlights.name: Nyishi and the hornbill hat
spotlights.spot_it: A cane helmet topped with the curved yellow casque of a hornbill, or now a fibreglass copy.
spotlights.story_md: The Nyishi are the largest group in Arunachal; their language is the mother tongue of about one person in five. A Nyishi man's ceremonial headgear, the **podum** or bopa, is a woven cane cap topped with the upper beak and casque of a great hornbill. Every hat meant a dead bird. Around Pakke, conservation groups and Nyishi village councils began handing out **fibreglass beaks** in the 2000s, and men swapped real ones for replicas. Today many men wear the copy, and the Pakke Paga Hornbill Festival, held in January at Seijosa, celebrates the bird alive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Culture and conservation found a compromise in one object.
spotlights.memory_hook: The beak on the hat is now fibreglass.

spotlights.name: Adi and the kebang
spotlights.spot_it: Men in cane helmets and red-and-white cloth sitting in a big raised bamboo hall, the village council in session.
spotlights.story_md: The Adi of the Siang valleys are known for their **kebang**, the village council that settles disputes, fixes festival dates and organises shared work. Councils of several villages form larger kebangs, and the Bogum Bokang Kebang is the apex body of the Adi. Adi villages also had a men's dormitory, the moshup, where boys learnt crafts, war and lore. Adi women dance the Ponung at Solung, the harvest festival. In 2024 and 2026 Adi villages in Upper Siang led the protests against a giant dam planned on their river.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how strong customary institutions still are, and why they matter in today's dam fight.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before the court, the kebang.

spotlights.name: Monpa of Tawang
spotlights.spot_it: Women in red-maroon tunics and black yak-hair caps with long tassels like spider legs.
spotlights.story_md: The Monpa of Tawang and West Kameng are Tibetan Buddhists, farmers and yak herders. The most recognisable thing they wear is a black cap of felted yak hair with long tassels that drain rain away from the face. They drink butter tea churned in a long wooden tube, make paper from the bark of a shrub, and dance the yak dance at Losar. The Monpa have long been a bridge between Tibet and India: the 6th Dalai Lama was the son of a Monpa woman, and Tawang's monks once followed Lhasa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tawang's identity, and India's case there, rest on the Monpa.
spotlights.memory_hook: A yak-hair hat with tassels to drain the rain.

spotlights.name: Idu Mishmi
spotlights.spot_it: A man with long hair tied in a top-knot, a bear-skin bag and a short sword, or women in black-and-red woven skirts.
spotlights.story_md: The Idu Mishmi live in the Dibang valley and around Roing. They are known for their priests, the **igu**, who chant through long night-time rituals, and for weaving: **Idu Mishmi textiles** received a Geographical Indication tag in 2019, with patterns that recall the Mishmi landscape and old stories. The Idu also have a taboo against killing tigers, which they regard as their elder brother. The proposed Dibang and Etalin dams, two of India's biggest, sit on Idu land, and the community has been divided over them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living belief that protects tigers, on land now wanted for dams.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Idu belief, the tiger is your elder brother.

spotlights.name: Wancho of Longding
spotlights.spot_it: Men with facial tattoos and carved wooden figures in a big village morung.
spotlights.story_md: The Wancho, about 57,000 people in Longding district in the Patkai hills, are related to the Konyak Naga across the border. Their villages were ruled by chiefs, the wangham, and their young men lived in morungs, dormitories carved with animals and human figures. Tattoos marked a man's life, including, in the past, success in raids: the Wancho were headhunters until the 20th century. Today their best-known craft is **wood carving**, and their most surprising recent achievement is an alphabet of their own, created by a schoolteacher.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A society that changed from raids to Unicode in about a century.
spotlights.memory_hook: From headhunting to a script in Unicode in one century.

compare.difference: The Nocte of Tirap are close relatives of the Wancho, but many Nocte became Vaishnava Hindus in the 19th century, while Wancho stayed animist or became Christian.

sections.title: Languages, and why everyone speaks Hindi
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal has more than thirty languages, most of them Tibeto-Burman, and many with only a few thousand speakers. In the 2011 census **Nyishi** was the largest mother tongue, at 20.7 per cent, followed by **Adi** at 17.4 per cent. Nepali (6.9) and Bengali (3.7) came from migrants. Hindi was the mother tongue of only 3.45 per cent.

Yet Hindi is how people from different tribes talk to each other. Census data shows 62.8 per cent of people speak Hindi as a first, second or third language, and officials estimate the real figure is higher. The official language of the state is English, which is the language of schools and offices.

Most local languages had no script of their own until the 20th century. Some now use Roman letters, some Tibetan, some new scripts.

spotlights.name: Arunachali Hindi
spotlights.spot_it: Listen in an Itanagar market: Hindi words, but with a grammar and accent all its own, and 'hai' at the end of everything.
spotlights.story_md: Arunachal is the one Northeastern state where Hindi became the common tongue. Several things pushed it. No single local language was big enough to unite the others, and many are not mutually intelligible. After 1962 the army, with its Hindi-speaking soldiers, ran roads, schools and hospitals in remote areas. Teachers from the Hindi belt staffed early schools, and traders from Rajasthan and Bihar ran the shops. The result is a local variety, sometimes called Arunachali Hindi, simplified and mixed with English and local words. Older people worry it is eating the tribal languages; younger people often speak Hindi better than their grandparents' tongue.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare case where Hindi spread without any state campaign, because people needed it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty languages, one market tongue: Hindi.

spotlights.name: The Wancho script
spotlights.spot_it: Rounded letters unlike any Indian or Roman script, on a chart in a Longding school.
spotlights.story_md: **Banwang Losu**, a middle-school teacher in Longding district, began designing an alphabet for the Wancho language in 2001 and finished it by about 2012. Until then Wancho had been written, if at all, in Roman or Devanagari letters that did not fit its sounds and tones. The script is taught in some schools, and in March 2019 it was added to **Unicode 12.0**, which means it works on phones and computers worldwide, with its own block of characters starting at U+1E2C0.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One teacher gave a small language a script, and the world's computers adopted it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A schoolteacher's alphabet made it into every phone.

sections.title: Faith
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal is the only Indian state where no religion has a majority. In 2011 Christians were 30.3 per cent, Hindus 29.0, followers of indigenous faiths such as Donyi-Polo 26.2, Buddhists 11.8 and Muslims 1.9.

Christianity grew fastest: from under 1 per cent in 1971 to about 30 per cent in 2011, mostly Baptist and Catholic, often through people's own networks rather than foreign missionaries, who were largely kept out. A 1978 state law against conversion by 'force or inducement' was passed but its rules were never framed for decades, and it remains a political fight.

The response from the Tani peoples was a revival: **Donyi-Polo**, the worship of sun and moon, was organised from the late 1960s into prayer halls, hymns and a flag. In the west, Tibetan Buddhism rules the landscape; in the east, Theravada Buddhism of the Tai Khamti and Singpho.

spotlights.name: Tawang Monastery
spotlights.spot_it: A white-walled monastery town on a ridge at about 3,000 m, with a golden roof and an 18-foot gilded Buddha inside.
spotlights.story_md: Tawang Monastery, Gaden Namgyal Lhatse, was founded in 1680 to 1681 by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso at the request of the 5th Dalai Lama. It is the largest Buddhist monastery in India. The story says the lama could not choose a site until his horse wandered off and was found standing on this ridge. Inside a wall 282 metres long are 65 residential buildings, a library of old scriptures and the main hall with a gilded Buddha about 5.5 metres high. In 1959 the 14th Dalai Lama stayed here after fleeing Tibet. In 1962 Chinese troops occupied the monastery for about six months and left it undamaged.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tawang is the main reason China claims Arunachal, and the main reason India will not let go.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lost horse chose the site of India's largest monastery.

spotlights.name: Golden Pagoda, Namsai
spotlights.spot_it: A gold Burmese-style stupa ringed by smaller gold spires, beside a lake in the eastern plains.
spotlights.story_md: The Golden Pagoda, **Kongmu Kham** in Tai Khamti, opened in 2010 at Tengapani in Namsai district. It was built on a 20-hectare site with money from Chowna Mein, the local MLA who later became deputy chief minister. It serves the Tai Khamti and Singpho, who are Theravada Buddhists, the tradition of Myanmar, Thailand and Sri Lanka, not the Tibetan Buddhism of Tawang. Its biggest festival is Kathina, when robes are given to monks after the rains. In April the Khamti celebrate Sangken, their water festival.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows that Arunachal has two Buddhisms, one facing Tibet and one facing Southeast Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tawang faces Lhasa; Namsai faces Mandalay.

spotlights.name: Donyi-Polo
spotlights.spot_it: A white flag with a red sun, seen above houses in Adi and Galo villages; prayer halls called gangging.
spotlights.story_md: Donyi-Polo means sun and moon, the eyes of the supreme being in Tani belief. Traditional Tani religion was a world of spirits handled by priests through sacrifice. From the late 1960s, led by **Talom Rukbo** (1937 to 2001), Adi reformers built it into an organised faith with weekly prayer halls, hymn books, images and a flag, partly to stop conversions to Christianity. The Donyi-Polo Yelam Kebang, its council, was formed in 1986. Today 31 December is celebrated as Donyi-Polo Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A traditional religion remade on the model of the big religions to survive.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sun and moon, given a flag and a hymn book.

spotlights.name: Parshuram Kund
spotlights.spot_it: Pilgrims in the cold Lohit river in January, at a pool among white boulders.
spotlights.story_md: Parshuram Kund lies on the Lohit river in Lohit district, about 48 km from Tezu. The legend: Parashurama killed his mother on his father's order, and the axe stuck to his hand until he washed it here. Each January, around Makar Sankranti, more than 70,000 pilgrims and sadhus come to bathe. The 1950 earthquake buried the original pool under boulders; the river later carved a new one. It is the main Hindu pilgrimage of the Northeast hills.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ties Arunachal into the sacred geography of Hindu India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The axe came off his hand only in the Lohit.

sections.title: Dance, music and festivals
sections.intro_md:
Almost every tribe has its own festival, usually tied to the farming year: sowing in spring, the first rice in summer, the harvest in autumn. The state government fixed common dates for many of them, so the calendar is full. Festivals are where you see the dress, the dances and the food at once, and where outsiders are usually welcome.

In the Buddhist west, the big events are **Losar**, the Tibetan new year, and **Torgya** at Tawang Monastery in January, with masked monastic dances. In the Tani centre the festivals belong to villages: Nyokum of the Nyishi in February, Mopin of the Galo in April, Dree of the Apatani in July and Solung of the Adi in September. And since 2012, a modern festival has put Ziro on the map of world music.

data.name: Donyi-Polo Day (31 Dec); Sunrise Festival, Dong

spotlights.name: Yak dance
spotlights.spot_it: A two-man yak costume, black and shaggy, ridden by a dancer in a mask, to drums and cymbals.
spotlights.story_md: The yak dance of the Monpa tells the story of how the yak was found: a hero, helped by a magical bird, discovered the animal that would let people live in the high valleys. Two men inside a costume of black yak hair play the yak, a masked rider climbs on its back, and other masked dancers circle it to the beat of drums and cymbals. It is danced at Losar and other Buddhist festivals in Tawang and West Kameng, and has been shown in Republic Day parades in Delhi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best-known dance of western Arunachal, and a celebration of the animal that makes high life possible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two men, one yak, and a rider who found it.

spotlights.name: Torgya
spotlights.spot_it: Monks in huge painted masks of deer, skeletons and wrathful gods dancing in the courtyard of Tawang Monastery in January.
spotlights.story_md: Torgya is held over three days in the eleventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually January, in the courtyard of Tawang Monastery. Monks in heavy masks and silk robes perform **cham**, slow, spinning ritual dances meant to drive away evil spirits and misfortune for the coming year. On the last day an effigy holding the year's evil is burned. Monpa families from across the district come in their best clothes. Every third year a bigger version, Dungyur, is held.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A masked monastic ritual you can watch, in India, in its home setting.
spotlights.memory_hook: Masks dance, evil burns, the year starts clean.

spotlights.name: Solung and the Ponung
spotlights.spot_it: A line of Adi women in white wraparounds and bead necklaces dancing in a circle around a lead singer with a sword.
spotlights.story_md: Solung is the Adi festival of the crops and the animals, held in early September, with dates set by each village kebang. It lasts several days: mithun and pigs are sacrificed, the stories of creation are sung, and families feast on rice beer and meat. Its signature dance is the **Ponung**, danced by women in a circle, led by a man called the miri who sings the verses and shakes a long iron sword with jingling discs. The songs can tell the whole origin of the world, so a Ponung can last all night.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The great harvest festival of the Siang, and a library of oral history in song.
spotlights.memory_hook: Women dance, a man with a jingling sword sings the creation.

spotlights.name: Dree
spotlights.spot_it: Apatani families in white and red in the paddy fields of Ziro in early July, praying for the rice.
spotlights.story_md: Dree is the Apatani festival of the crops, held around 5 July after the rice is planted. Priests make offerings to Tamu, Metii, Danyi and Harniang, the spirits who protect against pests, hunger and sickness, and families share cucumber, rice beer and rice cakes. Since the 1960s Dree has also become a big public event in Ziro, with cultural shows and a beauty pageant. In March the Apatani hold Myoko, a longer festival of friendship in which villages take turns hosting each other.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows how a farming ritual turned into a modern community festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Plant the rice in June, ask the gods to guard it in July.

spotlights.name: Ziro Festival of Music
spotlights.spot_it: Bamboo stages in a green rice valley, thousands in raincoats, indie bands and tribal folk singers on the same bill.
spotlights.story_md: The Ziro Festival of Music was started in 2012 by **Bobby Hano**, an Apatani music organiser, with partners from Delhi's indie scene. It is held each September in the Ziro valley, with stages built from bamboo by local Apatani crews and plastic banned on site. The bill mixes Indian indie bands, Northeast folk acts and international names; the 2025 edition, 25 to 28 September, had more than 45 artists, including Pandit Vishwa Mohan Bhatt and Lee Ranaldo of Sonic Youth. It is often called India's best outdoor music festival, and it has made Ziro a place people plan their year around.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The festival that turned a remote valley into a cultural destination.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sonic Youth in a rice valley with bamboo stages.

sections.title: Cane, cloth and paper
sections.intro_md:
Every household in rural Arunachal used to make most of what it used, and much of it from **cane and bamboo**: houses on stilts, floors, baskets, hats, fish traps, rain shields, bridges. Weaving on the backstrap loin loom is women's work across nearly all tribes, and each group has its own colours and motifs, so an expert can name a person's tribe from their shawl.

Two crafts are protected now. **Idu Mishmi textiles** received a GI tag in 2019, after Arunachal oranges. Apatani textiles followed in 2021. In Tawang, the Monpa paper made from bark was revived with government help in 2020. Masks, carved wood and metal work come from the Buddhist west and the Naga-related south-east.

visual.title: Objects from the RIWATCH museum, Roing

spotlights.name: Monpa handmade paper
spotlights.spot_it: Thick, fibrous, cream-coloured sheets, drying on frames in the sun, used for Buddhist scriptures and prayer flags.
spotlights.story_md: The Monpa make paper from the inner bark of a shrub they call **shugu sheng**. The bark is soaked, boiled, beaten to pulp, spread on a frame in water and dried in the sun. The paper, mon shugu, is strong and long-lasting, and was used for scriptures in monasteries and for prayer flags; the tradition is said to be about a thousand years old. Cheap Chinese paper nearly killed it. A 1994 revival failed. In December 2020 the Khadi and Village Industries Commission opened a unit in Tawang where nine trained artisans make 500 to 600 sheets a day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A craft that writes the holy books, saved from extinction in 2020.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bark becomes scripture.

spotlights.name: Idu Mishmi textiles
spotlights.spot_it: Black cloth with bands of red, yellow and white geometric motifs, worn as skirts, blouses and men's coats.
spotlights.story_md: Idu Mishmi women weave wraparound skirts (thuma), blouses (etopolo), men's sleeveless coats, bags and shawls on backstrap looms. Yarn was once spun from wild nettle; cotton and wool are common now. The patterns are named and carry meanings, some taken from the landscape and from the shaman's chants. In 2019 the Idu Mishmi Cultural and Literary Society won a Geographical Indication tag for the textiles, the second GI for the state after Arunachal oranges.
spotlights.why_it_matters: GI status protects a weaving tradition from machine-made copies.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nettle yarn, named patterns, a GI tag in 2019.

spotlights.name: Cane and bamboo
spotlights.spot_it: A conical carrying basket on a woman's back, held by a strap across the forehead; cane hats like helmets.
spotlights.story_md: In Arunachal, cane and bamboo are building material, furniture, tools and clothing. Baskets like the Adi **ebar** are carried on the back with a strap over the forehead and are woven tight enough to carry grain. Men wear cane helmets, sometimes with bear fur or hornbill beaks. Houses stand on stilts of wood and bamboo, with bamboo floors that let air through. Even the bridges were once cane: suspension bridges hung over the Siang and Subansiri, rebuilt by village labour after every flood.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The basic technology of the hills, still in daily use.
spotlights.memory_hook: House, hat, basket and bridge: all cane.

sections.title: Food and drink
sections.intro_md:
Arunachali food is simple, fresh and not oily. Rice is the base. Meat, especially pork, chicken, fish and mithun, is boiled or smoked over the fire in the kitchen, where it hangs for weeks. Fermented **bamboo shoot** sours many dishes. Green leaves come from the forest. Chillies are fierce, including the king chilli. Little oil and few spices are used, and many dishes are cooked in bamboo tubes or wrapped in leaves.

Rice beer is the social glue of the Tani peoples. In the west, Monpa food is Tibetan: noodles, dumplings, butter tea and cheese from yaks. The Tai Khamti in the east eat a Southeast Asian sticky rice. Two modern products have a Ziro address: a kiwi wine and an organic movement around valley farms.

spotlights.name: Apong (rice beer)
spotlights.spot_it: A milky or smoky-brown drink poured from a bamboo tube into a bamboo cup at every festival.
spotlights.story_md: Apong, also called opo or poka in different languages, is rice beer made at home, usually by women. Cooked rice, often with burnt rice husk ash for the dark kind, is mixed with a starter cake of rice and herbs and left to ferment for days in a basket or pot lined with leaves, then filtered through ash. It is offered to guests, to elders and to the spirits, and no festival, wedding or council meeting happens without it. Drinking it is a sign of trust; refusing it can be rude.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The drink that seals hospitality, prayer and politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: No kebang without apong.

spotlights.name: Fermented bamboo shoot
spotlights.spot_it: Pale shreds of bamboo with a strong sour smell, stored in jars or bamboo tubes, cooked with pork or fish.
spotlights.story_md: Young bamboo shoots are peeled, chopped and left to ferment for weeks, sometimes buried in pits lined with leaves. The result is sour and pungent, and keeps through the monsoon. It goes into pork curries, fish stews, chutneys and pika pila, an Apatani pickle of bamboo shoot, pork fat and chilli. Outsiders often find the smell hard; for many Arunachalis it is the taste of home. In the cities it is now sold in packets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The single flavour most people outside the region never expect.
spotlights.memory_hook: If it smells strong and sour, it is bamboo shoot.

spotlights.name: Thukpa
spotlights.spot_it: A big bowl of noodle soup with greens and meat or vegetables, steaming in a Tawang kitchen.
spotlights.story_md: Thukpa is Tibetan noodle soup, eaten across the Himalaya. In Tawang and West Kameng it is made with hand-pulled or local noodles, often of wheat or buckwheat, in a clear broth with greens, onion, ginger and garlic, and yak meat, pork or chicken. Monpa kitchens also make **zan**, a dense millet or maize porridge, and momos. Thukpa is what you eat after the drive over Sela.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday comfort food of the Buddhist west.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cross Sela, eat thukpa.

spotlights.name: Butter tea
spotlights.spot_it: Tea churned with butter and salt in a tall wooden cylinder, poured into small bowls and constantly refilled.
spotlights.story_md: Monpa households drink **butter tea**, tea boiled with salt and yak butter and churned in a tall wooden cylinder called a **changdung**. It is salty and rich, closer to soup than to sweet chai, and a host keeps refilling your cup. In the cold of Tawang and Mago it provides calories and fat. A well-made changdung, bound with metal bands, is a household treasure; one is kept in the RIWATCH museum at Roing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A survival food for altitude, wrapped in hospitality.
spotlights.memory_hook: Salty tea, churned in a wooden tube.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Most Arunachalis still live in villages, and village life is organised by custom more than by the state. Land is owned by clans and villages under customary law, and outsiders, including Indians from other states, cannot buy it. The **Inner Line Permit**, created in 1873, still requires Indians from outside to get a permit to enter; foreigners need a separate Protected Area Permit. Since the 2010s permits are issued online.

Councils such as the Adi kebang and the Apatani bulyang settle most disputes. Bride price, often in mithun, is common. Women do most of the farming and weaving and run the markets, but are rare in politics: only a handful have ever been elected to the 60-seat assembly.

Life is changing fast. Jhum fields are giving way to orchards, kiwi and cardamom. Young people move to Itanagar, Guwahati, Delhi and Bengaluru to study and work.

data.note: Indians from other states need one

spotlights.name: Rice and fish in one field
spotlights.spot_it: Flooded terraces fenced by bamboo and pine, with small fish flicking between the rice plants.
spotlights.story_md: The Apatani of Ziro farm wet rice on flat terraces fed by a careful network of channels from forest streams, without draught animals or machines. In June they release fingerlings, mostly common carp, into the flooded fields; the fish eat insects and weeds and fertilise the water, and are harvested with the rice. The valley's yields are high, and around it the Apatani keep managed pine and bamboo groves. Because of this system the Apatani Valley is on India's tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage status.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A thousand-year-old system that looks like modern sustainable farming.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Ziro, dinner swims in the rice field.

spotlights.name: Inner Line Permit
spotlights.spot_it: A printed or phone-screen permit checked at the gate on the road from Assam into Itanagar or Bhalukpong.
spotlights.story_md: The Inner Line was drawn by the British under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation of 1873, to stop plains traders and planters from moving into the hills and causing clashes. Independent India kept it. Any Indian from outside the state needs an Inner Line Permit to enter, for a fixed number of days; foreigners need a Protected Area Permit. Supporters say it protects tribal land and culture from being swamped by migrants, as happened in parts of the Northeast. Critics say it keeps out investment. The online e-ILP has made it a few clicks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The legal wall behind Arunachal's demographic and land protection.
spotlights.memory_hook: A colonial line from 1873 that still checks your phone.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal's public figures are mostly politicians, soldiers and mountaineers, and more recently musicians and athletes. A few names come up again and again.

**Pema Khandu**, the chief minister since 2016, is a Monpa from Tawang and the son of a former chief minister. **Kiren Rijiju**, a Union minister, is a Miji from West Kameng. **Tine Mena**, an Idu Mishmi, became the first woman from Arunachal to climb Everest, in 2011, and **Anshu Jamsenpa** of Bomdila climbed it twice in five days in 2017. **Taba Chake** writes songs in Nyishi, Hindi and English and fills stages at Ziro. Behind them stand figures like Talom Rukbo of the Donyi-Polo revival and Banwang Losu of the Wancho script.

spotlights.name: Pema Khandu
spotlights.spot_it: A broad-faced man in a Monpa jacket and cap, often seen playing football or singing.
spotlights.story_md: Pema Khandu was born in 1979, the son of Dorjee Khandu, chief minister from 2007 until he died in a helicopter crash in 2011. He became chief minister in July 2016 at 37 after a crisis in which the Congress government fell and was restored by the Supreme Court. Months later he took almost the whole party with him, first to a regional party and then to the BJP. In 2024 he was re-elected unopposed from Mukto in Tawang, the BJP won 46 of 60 seats, and he was sworn in for a third term on 13 June 2024. He is also known for singing on stage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The face of Arunachal's politics for a decade.
spotlights.memory_hook: Became chief minister at 37, then moved his government to a new party.

spotlights.name: Tine Mena
spotlights.spot_it: A young woman in a down suit with an ice axe, an Idu Mishmi from Dibang Valley.
spotlights.story_md: Tine Mena, from the Idu Mishmi community of Dibang Valley, climbed Mount Everest on 10 May 2011, becoming the first woman from Arunachal Pradesh and, by many accounts, from the Northeast to stand on the summit. She grew up far from any climbing scene and trained after joining an adventure course. She has since worked to bring young Arunachalis into mountaineering. In 2017 Anshu Jamsenpa from Bomdila became the first woman to climb Everest twice in one season, five days apart.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two Arunachali women hold Everest records.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Dibang Valley to the top of the world.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors take one of three routes. **The western circuit** goes from Bhalukpong over Bomdila and Dirang to Sela and Tawang, then up to the border lakes. **The central circuit** runs from Itanagar to Ziro, often timed for the music festival. **The eastern circuit** follows the Siang to Pasighat and the Lohit to Parshuram Kund, Walong and Dong. Namdapha is a world of its own in the south-east.

You need an Inner Line Permit, patience and time. Roads close in the monsoon. Mobile coverage disappears in valleys. Distances on the map lie: 300 kilometres can take two days.

spotlights.name: Bomdila
spotlights.spot_it: A town on a ridge at about 2,400 m, with a red-and-white monastery and apple orchards.
spotlights.story_md: Bomdila, the headquarters of West Kameng, sits about 2,400 metres up on the road to Tawang. Its Gentse Gaden Rabgye Ling monastery was built in 1965 as a copy of the Tsona Gontse monastery in southern Tibet, whose abbot had fled to India. In November 1962 Bomdila fell to Chinese troops, the deepest point of the attack in the west, and the news caused panic as far as Tezpur. Today it is a stop for tea, apple orchards and monastery murals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The town where the 1962 war reached its furthest point in the west.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bomdila fell in 1962; the panic reached Assam.

spotlights.name: Dirang
spotlights.spot_it: A stone fortress-village by a river in a warm valley, with hot springs and a yak research farm nearby.
spotlights.story_md: Dirang lies lower than Bomdila, at about 1,500 metres, in a sheltered valley of the Dirang river. Its old **dzong**, a stone fortified village said to date from the 17th century, was built to guard the route between Tawang and the plains. Nearby are hot springs, kiwi and apple orchards, and the National Research Centre on Yak at Nyukmadung. The Kalachakra gompa has painted ceilings with Vajrayana deities. It is where most travellers to Tawang break the journey.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A gentler valley between the passes, with a fort that guarded the Tawang trade route.
spotlights.memory_hook: A stone fort, a hot spring and a yak research farm.

spotlights.name: Ziro valley
spotlights.spot_it: A flat green bowl of rice fields at about 1,500 m, ringed by pine hills, with villages of bamboo houses packed close.
spotlights.story_md: Ziro is the plateau home of the Apatani, about 1,500 metres up in Lower Subansiri. Unlike most of Arunachal, it is flat: an old lake bed now covered with rice terraces, fishponds and bamboo groves. Apatani villages such as Hong, one of the largest in the state, pack hundreds of houses together on stilts. Visitors come for the Dree festival in July and the music festival in September, and to see the last tattooed grandmothers. The valley is on India's tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A cultural landscape recognised as one of a kind.
spotlights.memory_hook: A drained lake bed turned into Arunachal's best rice bowl.

sections.title: How the state earns
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal's economy is small: by PRS's estimate, per capita income in 2025-26 was about ₹3.1 lakh at current prices, above the Indian average of ₹2.5 lakh, and real growth was about 10 per cent. Agriculture contributed 27 per cent, industry 21 per cent and services 52 per cent. Most of the state budget comes from Delhi, through tax shares and grants, because the state raises little revenue of its own.

Farming has shifted from jhum toward cash crops: oranges (the first GI product of the state), large cardamom, kiwi, apples and tea. Tourism is growing fast from a small base. The big promise, and the big fight, is **hydropower**: the state's rivers could generate an estimated 50,000 megawatts or more, the highest potential in India. Dozens of dam agreements were signed in the 2000s. Few were built.

spotlights.name: Subansiri Lower dam
spotlights.spot_it: A huge concrete dam across a green river gorge at the border with Assam.
spotlights.story_md: The Subansiri Lower project, built by NHPC on the Arunachal-Assam border, is designed for 2,000 megawatts from eight 250 MW units. Work started in 2005. It was stopped from 2011 to 2019 by protests in Assam over safety and downstream floods, and by court cases. The first unit began commercial operation on 23 December 2025, a second in February 2026, and the rest are due by the end of 2026. Once complete it will be one of the largest hydropower stations in India. Upstream, NHPC is building the 2,880 MW Dibang dam, planned at about 278 metres as India's tallest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first of Arunachal's mega dams to produce power, after twenty years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Started 2005, first power 2025.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Three things dominate Arunachal's news in 2025 and 2026: **roads and tunnels to the border**, **dams on the Siang**, and **China**.

India is building at speed along the border: the Sela tunnel (2024), the Frontier Highway along the Line of Actual Control (approved at about ₹28,000 crore for some 1,640 km), and model villages under the Vibrant Villages programme. China, meanwhile, began building the world's largest hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo in July 2025, and keeps issuing Chinese names for places in the state; in April 2026 India again rejected the 'fictitious names'.

India's answer to the Chinese dam is a dam of its own, the **Siang Upper Multipurpose Project**, which Adi villages are fighting. In September and October 2026 the protests turned into clashes with police.

spotlights.name: Sela tunnel
spotlights.spot_it: Two tunnel portals below the snowline on the Tawang road, with army trucks rolling in.
spotlights.story_md: Before 2024 the only road to Tawang crossed Sela Pass at about 4,170 metres, often shut by snow for days. The Border Roads Organisation built two tunnels under the pass, at around 13,000 feet, about 1 km and 1.6 km long, with an escape tube, at a cost of about ₹825 crore. Prime Minister Modi opened them on 9 March 2024. Officials call it the world's longest twin-lane tunnel at that altitude. It shortens the drive and, more importantly for the army, keeps Tawang reachable all year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The road to Tawang no longer depends on the weather at Sela.
spotlights.memory_hook: Under Sela, not over it.

spotlights.name: The Siang Upper dam fight
spotlights.spot_it: Roadblocks of logs and banners in Adi villages in Upper Siang, with police and paramilitary lined up beyond.
spotlights.story_md: The Siang Upper Multipurpose Project is planned as India's largest dam, about 11,000 megawatts (reports range from 11,000 to 12,500), with around 9 billion cubic metres of storage. The government says it would produce power, and act as a buffer if China ever released or held back water upstream. Adi villages say it would drown their homes, fields and sacred sites. Since 2024 they have blocked the pre-feasibility survey. In September 2026 forces were deployed to Uggeng and Komkar, on 30 September protesters vandalised the local MLA's house in Yingkiong, and on 4 October police used batons at Uggeng. The chief minister invited the farmers' forum to talks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest development fight in the state, tangled up with China.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dam to answer a dam, on the Adi's river.

spotlights.name: China's Medog dam
spotlights.spot_it: Not visible from India: a construction site at the Great Bend of the Tsangpo, about 30 km from the border.
spotlights.story_md: On 19 July 2025 Chinese Premier Li Qiang attended the groundbreaking of the Medog, or Motuo, hydropower station in Nyingchi, Tibet, where the Yarlung Tsangpo drops through its great gorge before entering India. Planned at about 60,000 megawatts, roughly three times the Three Gorges Dam, it would be the largest hydropower project in the world, with reported costs above $160 billion. China says it is a run-of-river project within its rights. Chief Minister Khandu has called it an existential threat to the tribes of the Siang, and India has raised it with Beijing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Water, not only land, is now part of the India-China contest over Arunachal.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three Gorges times three, 30 km from the border.

spotlights.name: Names and passports
spotlights.spot_it: Lists of Chinese place names in Chinese state media, and an Indian passport held at a transit desk in Shanghai.
spotlights.story_md: China calls the state Zangnan and has issued 'standardised' Chinese names for places in it: six in 2017, fifteen in 2021, eleven in 2023, thirty in 2024, more in May 2025. India's foreign ministry rejects each round; in April 2026 it called the latest 'mischievous attempts' to give 'fictitious names'. China also gives stapled visas to some Arunachalis. On 21 November 2025 **Pema Wangjom Thongdok**, an Indian living in Britain and born in West Kameng, was held for about 18 hours at Shanghai Pudong during a transit, reportedly told her passport was invalid because of her birthplace. India lodged a strong protest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The claim is pressed through paperwork, not only soldiers.
spotlights.memory_hook: A birthplace on a passport became a diplomatic incident.

spotlights.name: Donyi Polo Airport
spotlights.spot_it: A terminal with a sloping roof shaped like a traditional house, at Hollongi south of Itanagar.
spotlights.story_md: Until 2022 Itanagar, a state capital, had no airport; travellers flew to Guwahati or Lilabari in Assam and drove. On 19 November 2022 Prime Minister Modi opened the **Donyi Polo Airport** at Hollongi, about 15 km from the capital, built by the Airports Authority of India on about 690 acres for about ₹645 crore, with a 2,300-metre runway. Its name honours the sun and moon of Tani belief. Flights now connect it to Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Guwahati.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gave the capital its first direct air link to the rest of India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A capital without an airport until 2022.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Arunachal is often described in one-liners. Some are wrong, some half right.

**'It is all one tribe.'** No: there are dozens of peoples with different languages, religions and histories, and they often want to be named precisely.

**'China took Arunachal in 1962 and gave it back.'** Half right: China occupied much of it for about a month and withdrew to roughly the McMahon Line, but never gave up its claim.

**'You cannot visit.'** Wrong: Indians need an Inner Line Permit, which is issued online; foreigners need a Protected Area Permit.

**'Hindi was imposed.'** Mostly wrong: it spread as a contact language between tribes, helped by the army, schools and traders, without any law.

**'Apatani nose plugs were banned by the government.'** Disputed: the clearest record credits the Apatani Youth Association's call in 1974.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
**Where:** the north-eastern corner of India, between Bhutan, Tibet and Myanmar; 83,743 km², 1.38 million people (2011), 17 per km², the emptiest state.

**Who:** dozens of peoples. Tani groups (Nyishi, Adi, Galo, Apatani) in the centre, Buddhist Monpa in the west, Mishmi in the east, Naga-related Wancho, Nocte and Tangsa in the south-east, Theravada Tai Khamti on the eastern plains.

**History:** Chutia brick forts in the foothills, Tibetan Buddhism in Tawang (monastery 1680 to 1681), the McMahon Line (1914), NEFA (1954), the war of 1962, statehood (1987).

**See it:** Apatani nose plugs, the Nyishi hornbill hat, the yak dance, Torgya masks, the Golden Pagoda, rice-fish terraces at Ziro, the great hornbill.

**Now:** the Sela tunnel, the Siang dam fight, China's Medog dam, Chinese place names, and the first Sunrise Festival at Dong.

best_facts.fact: In the 1880s a Lepcha tailor named Kinthup, after being sold twice as a slave in Tibet, threw 500 marked logs into the Tsangpo to prove it became the Brahmaputra. Nobody was watching downstream: his officer had died.
best_facts.why_surprising: Heroic proof, completely wasted, then vindicated 30 years later.

best_facts.fact: The 6th Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, was born near Tawang in 1683 to a Monpa mother and is remembered for writing love songs.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Dalai Lama who preferred poetry and romance, born in today's India.

best_facts.fact: The Bugun liocichla was described as a new species in 2006 by Ramana Athreya, an astrophysicist, without killing a bird. One survey counted only 14 of them.
best_facts.why_surprising: New birds are still being found in India, by astronomers.

best_facts.fact: Only 3.45 per cent of Arunachalis have Hindi as their mother tongue, yet it is the language people of different tribes use with each other.
best_facts.why_surprising: Hindi spread here without any campaign, in the Northeast.

best_facts.fact: Sela Pass and Nuranang Falls are said to be named after Sela and Nura, two Monpa girls who helped Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat in his last stand in November 1962.
best_facts.why_surprising: Place names on the Tawang road are a war story.

best_facts.fact: Namdapha National Park holds four big cats: tiger, leopard, clouded leopard and snow leopard.
best_facts.why_surprising: Few parks on Earth span jungle to snowline.

best_facts.fact: Nyishi men around Pakke swapped real hornbill beaks on their ceremonial hats for fibreglass copies.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tradition kept its look and dropped its cost to wildlife.

best_facts.fact: A middle-school teacher, Banwang Losu, created an alphabet for the Wancho language; it entered Unicode in 2019.
best_facts.why_surprising: One person's script now works on every phone.

best_facts.fact: Dong, in Anjaw district, sees India's first sunrise; in June the sun comes up there around 4 a.m. by Indian Standard Time.
best_facts.why_surprising: One time zone for a country 3,000 km wide.

best_facts.fact: China's Medog hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo, begun on 19 July 2025, is planned at about 60,000 MW, three times the Three Gorges Dam, about 30 km from the Indian border.
best_facts.why_surprising: The world's biggest dam, upstream of Arunachal.

best_facts.fact: Arunachal has 17 people per square kilometre, the lowest density of any Indian state. India's average is 382.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state as big as Austria with fewer people than Lucknow.

best_facts.fact: Among the Adi, a marriage is not settled until the groom's family gives the bride's household at least one mithun.
best_facts.why_surprising: A half-wild bovine is a bank account and a bride price.

best_facts.fact: In 2024, ten of Arunachal's 60 MLAs, including Chief Minister Pema Khandu, were elected unopposed.
best_facts.why_surprising: One in six seats had no contest.

best_facts.fact: Tawang Monastery's site was chosen, the story says, by the founder's horse, which wandered off and was found standing on the ridge.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's largest monastery, sited by a horse.

best_facts.fact: The Apatani grow rice and fish in the same flooded field, without draught animals or machines; the valley is on India's tentative list for World Heritage.
best_facts.why_surprising: Ancient farming that reads like a sustainability textbook.

best_facts.fact: The Stilwell Road from Ledo to Kunming, built 1942 to 1945 and passing through Arunachal, cost more than 1,100 American lives: 'a man a mile'.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Second World War front line ran through this state.

best_facts.fact: Christians were under 1 per cent of Arunachal's people in 1971 and about 30 per cent in 2011; no religion has a majority.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the fastest religious shifts anywhere in India.

best_facts.fact: The Arunachal macaque, described in 2005, takes its scientific name from the Monpa word munzala, 'deep-forest monkey'.
best_facts.why_surprising: A new primate species in the 21st century.

On the evening of **15 August 1950**, India's third Independence Day, the ground under the eastern Himalaya broke. The epicentre was near Rima in Tibet, just north of today's Arunachal, and the magnitude was about **8.6**, which makes it one of the largest earthquakes ever recorded on land.

Why so big? India's plate is pushing north into Asia at about 4 to 5 centimetres a year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow. The rocks on the boundary lock, store that strain for centuries, then slip all at once. Here, at the eastern corner where the Himalaya bends south into the Burmese ranges, the slip ran along a fault hundreds of kilometres long.

The shaking was only the start. Thousands of landslides poured into the Siang, Dibang, Lohit and Subansiri. Some blocked rivers completely and formed lakes. Days later these natural dams burst, and walls of water, mud and trees went down into Assam, raising riverbeds and flooding towns. Parshuram Kund, the Hindu pilgrimage pool on the Lohit, was buried under boulders; the river later cut a new one.

Survivors across the region reported loud explosive sounds. Deaths are estimated at about 1,500 to 4,800 across India and Tibet, low for its size because the region was so empty.

Engineers still use 1950 as a design case for every dam proposed on these rivers. When you read about the Siang or Dibang dams, remember that the same mountains have done this before.

offline_task.title: Make a Tawang-style thukpa
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2. About 30 minutes.**

**You need**
- 150 g flat wheat noodles (or any thick noodles)
- 200 g chicken or pork, thinly sliced, or 200 g mixed vegetables and tofu for a vegetarian version
- 1 onion, 1 tomato, 4 cloves garlic, 1 inch ginger, 1 or 2 green chillies
- A handful of greens: spinach, mustard leaves or bok choy
- Salt, a little soy sauce, a pinch of Sichuan pepper or black pepper, oil
- 1 litre water or stock

**Steps**
1. Pound or grind the garlic, ginger and chillies to a rough paste.
2. Heat a spoon of oil in a deep pot. Fry the sliced onion until soft, then the paste for a minute.
3. Add the meat and stir until it changes colour. Add the chopped tomato and cook until soft.
4. Pour in the water or stock, add salt and a splash of soy, and simmer 15 minutes.
5. Meanwhile, boil the noodles separately until just done; drain.
6. Add the greens to the soup for the last two minutes. Season with pepper.
7. Put noodles in deep bowls and ladle the soup over.

**Notice**: thukpa should taste clean and gingery, not oily or heavily spiced. In Tawang it is eaten after a cold day; serve it hot and drink the broth.
